finding.claim: DELETE /projects/:id calls authorized(), which only returns a boolean, and ignores the result. Any authenticated user can delete any project. The sibling route uses authorize(), which throws, so this looks like a mix-up of the two helpers.
finding.source: Any authenticated user sends DELETE /projects/<id> for a project they don't own, with req.user not admin.

trace.note: Route handler for DELETE /projects/:id. The only guard is authentication, which is assumed to run upstream.
Project is loaded by the attacker-supplied id. There is no ownership filter.
authorized(req.user, project) returns false for non-owners, but the return value is discarded and nothing throws.
Returns 204, so the attacker sees success.

finding.guards_checked: Checked authorized() at api.js:12-14. It is a pure predicate with no side effects and no throw. Only one file exists in the directory, so there is no middleware here and I could not see any upstream authorization. Checked whether the call is wrapped in a conditional or throw. It is not.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: authorized() at api.js:12-14 is a pure boolean predicate whose result is discarded at api.js:18; authorize() (api.js:4-10, which throws) is only used on the PUT route at api.js:25. No middleware is visible in the directory (only api.js exists).
verdict.reason: api.js:18 calls the boolean-returning authorized() as a bare statement, so nothing throws or returns early and api.js:19 deletes the project for any authenticated non-owner, non-admin user. The PUT route at api.js:25 uses the throwing authorize(), which confirms the mix-up.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none effective: authorized() at api.js:12-14 is a pure boolean predicate whose result is discarded at api.js:18; the throwing authorize() (api.js:4-10) is only used in the PUT route at api.js:25.
verdict_facts.reason: api.js:18 calls the boolean-returning authorized() as a bare statement and never checks the result, so any authenticated non-owner, non-admin reaches req.store.projects.delete at api.js:19 and gets a 204 at api.js:20.

finding.claim: A non-existent project id likely makes projects.get() return undefined, because the store looks like a Map. Dereferencing it (project.id at line 19, and ownerId inside authorize at line 5) throws a TypeError. In the DELETE route the throw happens at line 19, after the missed authorization check. This is mainly a robustness problem, and Express 4 may turn it into a 500 response. It is low severity, and it is not a security finding by itself.
finding.source: The :id path parameter is an arbitrary string supplied by the attacker.
finding.sink: Unhandled TypeError at api.js:19 and api.js:5.

trace.note: get() on an unknown id returns undefined, assuming Map semantics.
authorize() reads resource.ownerId on undefined and throws a TypeError, giving 500 instead of 404.

finding.guards_checked: No null check, 404 handling, or error middleware is visible in this file. The store implementation is not in scope, so I could not confirm its behavior.

verdict.guard_found: none in api.js: no null check or 404 handling on the get() result (api.js:17, 24). authorize() (api.js:4-10) throws on failure. authorized() (api.js:12-14) returns a bool, and the DELETE route discards it at api.js:18. No error middleware is in this file.
verdict.reason: Lines 17 and 25 are accurate, but the claim that the DELETE throw happens at api.js:19 is wrong: authorized() at api.js:18 would throw at api.js:13 first. Whether get() returns undefined depends on req.store, which isn't in scope (api.js:17), and the result at most gives a 500 instead of a 404, which is not a security issue.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (no null check or 404 handling in api.js; the store, and any error middleware, are outside this directory)
verdict_facts.reason: The claim that DELETE throws at api.js:19 is wrong: if get() at api.js:17 returns undefined, authorized() at api.js:18 throws first, at api.js:13. Whether get() returns undefined for an unknown id depends on req.store, which isn't in this directory. Even if it does, the result is a non-security robustness error.
